# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

# Review: "Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem" (Varga & Holm, Comment)

Sections 1–5 are a useful re-analysis. They use the microdata to confirm, with numbers, several problems that could only be suspected from the Halden working paper, and the attrition finding is new and important.

Sections 6–8 and the Conclusion go well beyond the evidence. The claim that per-hour gains are "entirely an artifact" is not supported by the comment's own analysis. It also ignores the one randomised result that contradicts it.

**Arithmetic.** Table 2 checks out: 95.1/0.8 = +18.9%, 98.4/0.859 = +14.6%, 95.4/0.861 = +10.8%. The hours falls (−14.1%, −13.9%) and the real revenue figure (1.014/1.041 − 1 ≈ −2.6%) are also correct. There are two arithmetic problems:

- **The hours decomposition doesn't add up (§3).** Four days at +0.7 hours each, plus 1.6 hours on the day off, gives 32 + 2.8 + 1.6 = **36.4** hours a week, not the reported 34.6. If 1.6 hours of day-off work is right, the four remaining days were longer by only about 0.25 hours each. One of the figures is wrong.
- **The novelty extrapolation is off (§6).** Energy fell 0.32 SD between months 3 and 6, about 0.107 a month. At that rate the remaining 0.29 SD is gone in about 2.7 more months, i.e. around **month 8.7**, not "around month ten."

## What the comment gets right

- **Attrition (§1).** This is the most important new finding. The working paper said the nine organisations withdrew "during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons." According to the microdata, seven withdrew *after the schedule began*, and six cited workload or output.
  - That is a material misstatement in the original paper, and Halden should correct it.
  - Under intention-to-treat, those seven are treated organisations whose outcomes are missing.
  - Minor: six cited workload and two cited scheduling, which accounts for eight of the nine. Say what the ninth gave.
- **Manager index versus records (§2).** In 19 of 23 organisations the manager's index was higher than the record-based index. A sign test gives p ≈ 0.003 (two-sided), so this is strong evidence of a systematic upward bias. The framing ("we do not suggest bad faith") is fair.
  - One caveat should be stated. Records may capture only part of output, such as a single countable metric, so the record-based index is not automatically the truth. The bias is very likely real, but its size is less certain than "four points" implies.
- **Hours denominator (§3), revenue (§4), and the mechanical per-hour metric (§5).** These are correct and well documented.

## Problems

### 1. The abstract says attrition was corrected; it wasn't

The abstract says "Correcting the first three [problems]," and the first three are attrition, the output measure and hours. Table 2 corrects only output and hours. The 10.8% figure is still computed on survivors only.

The attrition bias probably points downward, but its size is never estimated. Possible approaches include worst-case or Lee bounds, or plausible imputed outcomes for the seven organisations that started and then withdrew. Either do this or remove the claim from the abstract.

### 2. Table 2 mixes changes in the sample with the corrections

Each row uses a different sample: 61, 23, 27 and 17 organisations. The fall from +23.4% to +10.8% therefore mixes two things: the effect of each correction, and differences between subsets.

All four specifications should be computed on the same 17 organisations. That way the decomposition is like-for-like and the reader can see each correction's contribution. The Data Note admits the subsets are non-random, but the abstract and conclusion still compare 10.8% against 23.4% as if they described the same sample.

There is also no confidence interval on the 10.8%, which rests on 17 self-selected organisations.

### 3. Revenue isn't part of the per-hour gain

The abstract says four problems "account for most of the reported gain," and lists revenue as one of them. But revenue never enters the per-hour calculation. The real-terms correction is a fair criticism of how the working paper presented revenue, but it doesn't account for any of the 23.4%.

A smaller point: CPI is a consumer-price deflator. Output or producer prices for each sector would be the right deflator for organisational revenue.

### 4. The novelty argument doesn't support "entirely an artifact"

- **The extrapolation is weak.** It rests on two survey points, a linear extrapolation, and the arithmetic error noted above. It also assumes that self-reported energy tracks productivity, which the comment never shows.
- **The direct test is in the comment's own data and wasn't run.** The pilot collected the output index *monthly*. If the per-hour gain is a novelty effect, output should decline over months 1–6, at least in the 17-organisation subset with actual hours. The comment should report that trend rather than infer the decline from a survey measure.
- **Varden partly addresses the novelty argument.** Its staff were randomised and did not choose the change, so the "staff chose and welcomed it" part of the novelty story doesn't apply there. Varden also reported at nine months, roughly when the comment's own extrapolation says energy should be back at baseline. It still found +12.5% per actual hour.
- **"The burden of proof lies with those claiming [durability]"** justifies calling the gain *unproven*. It does not justify calling it *entirely an artifact*. Not having evidence that a gain lasts is different from having evidence that it doesn't exist.

### 5. Varden is cited selectively

The comment calls Varden's counter-stratum result "the most reliable finding in the literature," but never mentions Varden's case-processing stratum. That stratum found **+12.5% (95% CI +6.9 to +18.4) per actual hour**, and it avoids every problem the comment identifies:

| Problem raised in the comment | Varden case-processing |
|---|---|
| Self-selection / attrition | Randomised; no attrition reported |
| Manager-rated output | Administrative records |
| Scheduled-hours denominator | Timesheet actual hours |
| No comparison group | Concurrent control offices |
| Revenue proxy | Not used |

Its effect is also close to the comment's own corrected Halden figure (+10.8%). Two studies with very different designs agreeing on a gain of roughly 11–12% in backlog-type work is evidence *for* a real effect, not against one.

There is also some irony in which stratum the comment praises. The counter stratum had the widest intervals in Varden, came from 5 v 5 offices with the few-cluster problem discussed earlier, and measured output per *employee*. A fall in output per employee doesn't contradict a gain in output per hour. As Varden itself argued, the two measures separate in coverage-bound work.

### 6. The criticism of the meetings analysis is partly unfair, and the standard is applied unevenly

- **Varden is misdescribed.** The seven offices were not "selected for analysis after the results were known." They are *all* the treated case-processing offices. The data were collected at month six at managers' request, before the nine-month results.
- **Varden already made the comment's point.** It said the analysis was unregistered, that seven offices "cannot establish a mechanism," and that a confirmatory test was registered. Varden's summary does say meetings "may account for part" of the gain, so a warning against citing this as a mechanism is reasonable. But the comment is arguing against a stronger claim than Varden made.
  - The valid criticism is a different one: Varden had only month-six calendar data, so it could not measure how much each office *cut* its meetings.
- **The standard is applied unevenly.** The comment rejects an exploratory correlation across seven offices that its authors clearly labelled as exploratory. It then puts forward its own novelty explanation, based on extrapolating two survey points, as part of its *conclusion*. Both are hypotheses and should be treated the same way.

### 7. The sectoral claims rest on small numbers

The 11.2% fall in retail and hospitality output comes from three organisations. Compare it with the manager index *for those same three* rather than the 93.1 for all six.

"Where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output" is supported only for the case where staffing and opening hours are held fixed, as in Varden. Say so.

## Suggested revisions

1. **Abstract.** Remove "correcting the first three," or actually correct for attrition using bounds. Drop revenue from the list of problems that account for the gain.
2. **Table 2.** Compute every specification on the 17-organisation subset, and add intervals.
3. **§3.** Reconcile the hours decomposition with the 34.6 total.
4. **§6.** Test for decay using the monthly output index. Fix the month-ten extrapolation. Treat novelty as a hypothesis.
5. **§5 and §8.** Discuss Varden's case-processing result, and note that it agrees with the corrected Halden figure.
6. **§7.** Describe Varden's analysis accurately. Recast the section as "not yet evidence of mechanism" rather than "post hoc subgroup fitting."
7. **Conclusion.** Replace "entirely an artifact" with something like:

> "Correcting for manager-rated output and scheduled hours roughly halves the reported per-hour gain, to about 11% in a non-random subset, before any adjustment for attrition, which likely lowers it further. Whether the remainder is durable is unknown. Randomised evidence finds a similar per-hour gain in backlog-type work and a loss of output per employee in coverage-bound work."

The recommendations for future evaluations at the end of the comment are sound and should be kept as they are.

I can also put together a one-page synthesis of what the three documents together support, if that would help.
